text: So in the modern agent applications, inputs are often very long.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It easily exceeds 10k tokens while outputs are relatively short.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And more importantly, a large portion of the inputs are repeated across requests.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In many real workloads, like 50% to 80% to 90% of the tokens are identical across different requests.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So from a system perspective, this means most of the compute cost is in the pre-filled stage, where the model processes the entire inputs and build a KB cache.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if we recompute this shared prefix every time, you're wasting both latency and GPU cycles.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So when a new recast share a prefix with the previous one, we can reuse those tensor and skip the corresponding preferred computation and directly reduce the TTFT and we can avoid computing large chunk of the input.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But however, making this work at scale requires two key mechanisms.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So first one is cache-aware routing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in the distributed system, KVCache is not centralized.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It lives on individual replicas.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the router must send incoming requests to the replica that already holds the relevant prefix in its cache.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Otherwise, we lose the benefit of reuse.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second thing is cache hierarchy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So KVCache is extremely memory intensive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For large models and long contacts, KVCache size can exceed model weights.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And as you know, GPU VRAM is the fastest, but there's also very limited resources.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we treat cache as a hierarchy, like hot cache stays in GPU memory, worm cache is in CPU RAM, and cordial cache can be offloaded to NVMe or the disk spaces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The system dynamically offloads less used blocks and prepares them when they need it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So by combining cache-aware routing and hierarchical memory management, we significantly reduce the prefix calls, lower TTFT, and making long-context agent workload much more efficient.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the next thing is interactive speed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So standard autoregressive decoding, it generates one token per forward pass that makes decode inherently a sequencer, and during the decode, the GPU is often underutilized.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And speculative decoding changes the shape of this problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So instead of generating one token and stopping, it proposes multiple candidates' tokens ahead.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then the target model validates those candidates in a single pass, and if the tokens are accepted, they are free.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this improves time per output token without changing model's output quality.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There are different ways to draft candidates.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one way is model-based speculation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It uses a small draft model to predict the future tokens, and the benefit of it is it can achieve higher acceptance rate, but the cost is the extra compute.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And another method is model-free speculation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It uses pattern from a prompt or prior output, so it has lower overhead
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But it works best only when the output resembles the existing context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the important part is the tradeoff.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So speculation can improve per request latency, but validation as overhead to the batch.

text: So the best strategy is not static.
